nodes.title: Electrical basics
nodes.why: Understanding voltage, current, and circuits is needed to wire and test instrumentation.
checkpoints: Ohm's law states V = I × R, so increasing resistance lowers current at constant voltage.
A series circuit adds resistances, so total resistance equals sum of individual resistances.
A short circuit creates very low resistance, causing excessive current flow that can trip protective devices.

nodes.title: Instrumentation fundamentals
nodes.why: Knowing how common sensors work enables accurate calibration and troubleshooting.
checkpoints: Pressure transducers convert pressure into a proportional electrical signal, often 4-20 mA.
Thermocouples generate voltage proportional to temperature difference between junctions, requiring cold-junction compensation.
Vibration sensors such as accelerometers output voltage proportional to acceleration, useful for monitoring rotating equipment.

nodes.title: Safety fundamentals
nodes.why: Proper lockout, tagout, and fall protection keep technicians safe while working on equipment.
checkpoints: Lockout-tagout isolates energy sources, preventing accidental start-up while work is performed.
Fall protection harnesses arrest a fall by distributing load, reducing injury risk.
Arc flash boundaries define distance where thermal exposure can cause burns, requiring PPE.

nodes.title: PLC basics
nodes.why: Reading ladder logic lets technicians interpret control programs linked to field devices.
checkpoints: Ladder logic uses rungs that represent logical operations, where contacts act as inputs and coils as outputs.
A PLC scan cycle reads inputs, executes logic, then updates outputs, typically within tens of milliseconds.
Bit addresses in PLC programs refer to specific I/O points, enabling direct control of field devices.

nodes.title: Sensor calibration and troubleshooting
nodes.why: Calibrating and fixing pressure, temperature, and vibration sensors ensures reliable turbine and substation data.
checkpoints: Calibration verifies that a sensor’s output matches a known standard, adjusting span or zero as needed.
If a pressure sensor reads high at zero pressure, the zero offset may be misadjusted.
Replacing a faulty vibration sensor restores accurate acceleration signals, preventing false alarms.

nodes.title: 4‑20 mA loop tracing
nodes.why: Tracing current loops identifies wiring faults that affect sensor signals to the SCADA system.
checkpoints: A 4-20 mA loop supplies constant current, so any break causes the receiver to see 0 mA.
Measuring voltage across a resistor in the loop determines current using Ohm's law.
Loop testing with a multimeter can locate open circuits by checking for expected voltage drop.

nodes.title: Modbus communication
nodes.why: Understanding Modbus lets technicians verify that field devices transmit data correctly to SCADA.
checkpoints: Modbus RTU transmits data in frames with address, function code, and CRC for error checking.
Reading a holding register via Modbus retrieves the current sensor value from the device.
If a Modbus response has an invalid CRC, the master discards the message and may retry.

nodes.title: Reading P&IDs and schematics
nodes.why: Interpreting diagrams allows technicians to locate and service the correct instrumentation.
checkpoints: P&IDs show process equipment and instrumentation symbols, linking loops to physical devices.
Loop diagrams detail signal flow from field sensor through transmitters to control system.
Electrical schematics display wiring connections, enabling identification of circuit breakers and fuses.

nodes.title: LOTO and height safety
nodes.why: Applying lockout‑tagout and fall protection prevents accidents during maintenance at elevation.
checkpoints: Lockout devices physically prevent operation, and tags warn personnel of the locked condition.
When working above 2 meters, harnesses must be anchored to a suitable load‑bearing point.
Conducting a pre‑task safety briefing reduces the chance of procedural oversights.

nodes.title: SCADA trend analysis
nodes.why: Analyzing trends helps detect equipment degradation before it causes unplanned downtime.
checkpoints: SCADA trend lines plot sensor values over time, revealing gradual deviations that indicate wear.
A sudden drop in vibration amplitude may signal a sensor fault, prompting inspection before failure.
Predictive alerts can be configured to trigger work orders when a parameter exceeds a set threshold.

nodes.title: Maintenance record keeping
nodes.why: Documenting work orders and calibration results creates traceable equipment history.
nodes.quote: Write clear work orders and calibration records
checkpoints: Work orders assign a unique identifier, linking tasks to specific assets for traceability.
Calibration records must include date, instrument identification, and measured versus expected values.
Updating the maintenance system after a task ensures equipment history is current for future analysis.

nodes.title: Solar inverter knowledge
nodes.why: Knowing inverter operation supports work on solar sites and integration with control systems.
checkpoints: Solar inverters convert DC from panels to AC, employing maximum power point tracking to optimize output.
Inverters communicate status via protocols like Modbus or CAN bus, allowing remote monitoring.
If an inverter’s input voltage exceeds limits, it will shut down to protect downstream equipment.

nodes.title: Wind turbine controller knowledge
nodes.why: Understanding turbine controllers aids troubleshooting of turbine-specific instrumentation.
checkpoints: Wind turbine controllers manage blade pitch and generator torque based on wind speed measurements.
Controllers use supervisory control logic to activate brakes during overspeed events.
A fault in the yaw control system can misalign the rotor, reducing power capture.
